summary:
Canada's federal framework prohibits discrimination and hate-motivated conduct on grounds of gender identity and gender expression. Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017, added both grounds to the Canadian Human Rights Act and to the Criminal Code's hate-motivation provisions, and courts have applied them consistently since. Provincial human-rights statutes reinforce the federal layer. Ontario's Human Rights Code expressly covers gender identity and gender expression.

No Canadian jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities. Legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration. Prince Edward Island's 2016 amendment to its Vital Statistics Act replaced the surgery requirement with a declaration of one's identified gender supported by a doctor's letter, and federal identity documents can carry an X marker. Entry carries no trans-specific friction.

Provincial governments have moved in the opposite direction on schools and sport. Saskatchewan's Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act of 2023, adopted invoking the notwithstanding clause, requires schools to obtain parental consent before students under 16 may use a gender-related preferred name or express a gender identity. Alberta passed a Health Statutes Amendment Act, an Education Amendment Act and the Fairness and Safety in Sport Act in 2024, then shielded them from legal challenge through Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025, again using the notwithstanding clause. Human-rights groups have called for repeal of the Saskatchewan measure, and legal action followed.

Conditions in custody are the least settled area of trans-specific policy. After Bill C-16, transgender prisoners are to be assigned to correctional institutions on the basis of their gender identity, and prisoners held for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for gender-affirming surgery. Placement and gender-affirming treatment have both been contested in Canadian courts, including litigation brought on behalf of trans prisoner Synthia Kavanagh over medical treatment and assignment to a women's institution. A 2022 report alleged that gender-diverse prisoners face a pattern of abuse and discrimination in Canadian jails and are more likely to be victims of sexual assault.
tangentialFactors:
Statistics Canada's release of 30 March 2026 records 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents in 2024, a 1% increase after a 34% jump in 2022-23. Incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, down from a 2023 peak of 889, ending three consecutive years of increases. That release does not break out incidents motivated by gender identity separately from sexual orientation.

Canada is routinely positioned against the direction of travel elsewhere. Reporting on the 2017 Senate vote framed Bill C-16 as leadership amid a global anti-LGBT backlash. Egale Canada has published analysis of 2024 police-reported hate crime affecting 2SLGBTQI people in Canada, and the federal 2SLGBTQI+ Action Plan survey findings are published as quick statistics.
localsOnly:
Discrimination recourse runs through provincial human-rights bodies. The Ontario Human Rights Commission publishes policy setting out the legal context, case law and legislation for complaints under the Ontario Human Rights Code, which expressly covers gender identity and gender expression; the same machinery serves residents and complainants generally.

Every level of government regulates school climate. Ontario's Accepting Schools Act of 2012 addresses bullying including LGBTQ students, and comparable anti-bullying statutes exist in Quebec, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Alberta, Newfoundland and Labrador, the Northwest Territories and Yukon. Custodial policy facing residents rather than visitors includes the federal identity-based placement rule and the 12-month threshold for consideration of gender-affirming surgery. A 2022 study of Nova Scotia correctional officers found them generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety and security, while recording some officer concern about risk to other prisoners.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the gaps against the Yogyakarta Principles identified in Egale Canada's 2012 UPR submission have since closed is unresolved here; that submission predates Bill C-16 and the current federal discrimination framework, and no later assessment of the same benchmark is cited.

The 2022 report alleging a pattern of abuse of gender-diverse prisoners in Canadian jails is a reported finding rather than an adjudicated determination, and no official response or case outcome is sourced. The Statistics Canada release gives no gender-identity breakdown of hate-crime motivation, so the volume of trans-targeted incidents in 2024 is not established. The federal X-marker process and any supporting documentation requirements are not documented in the sources currently cited. Whether the notwithstanding-clause-shielded Alberta measures face renewed challenge after Bill 9 is also unresolved.
